The Case for Raising the Impeachment Threshold: Depoliticizing Constitutional Judgment

The impeachment and removal of federal officials stands as one of the most consequential powers vested in the American constitutional system. Designed as a mechanism of last resort to address grave abuses of public trust, it carries the weight of democratic sovereignty and the stability of the republic. Yet in recent decades, the process has been increasingly wielded not as a solemn safeguard against tyranny or corruption, but as a routine instrument of partisan combat. To preserve institutional legitimacy, restore the gravity of constitutional removal, and shield the federal government from the destabilizing effects of political weaponization, the United States must amend the Constitution to significantly raise the threshold required for the conviction and removal of federal officials. By elevating the supermajority requirement and embedding structural safeguards that compel bipartisan consensus, the impeachment process can be reclaimed from partisan opportunism and realigned with its original purpose: a national judgment, not a political tally.

The Founders understood the inherent dangers of impeachment. In Federalist No. 65, Alexander Hamilton warned that the process would inevitably agitate the passions of the community and divide it into factions aligned with rival political champions. Recognizing this vulnerability, the Constitutional Convention deliberately placed the power of trial in the Senate and required a two-thirds majority for conviction. At the time, this threshold was exceptionally high in an era of cross-cutting political alliances and weaker party discipline. The Framers assumed that removing an elected or appointed official would demand overwhelming evidence, broad deliberation, and genuine national consensus. Today, however, highly polarized party systems, disciplined legislative caucuses, and a media ecosystem that rewards procedural warfare have effectively lowered the practical barrier to conviction. What was designed as a rare national referendum on official conduct has become susceptible to majority-party maneuvering and minority-party counter-weaponization, eroding public trust with each politically charged proceeding.

Raising the constitutional threshold for removal to three-fourths of the Senate, or alternatively requiring that a conviction include a specified minimum number of votes from both major parties, would restore the process’s intended gravity. A higher threshold acts as a structural filter against partisan capture. It forces legislators to look beyond caucus loyalty and evaluate evidence through the lens of enduring constitutional standards rather than electoral calculus. When removal demands near-consensus, politically motivated accusations are naturally winnowed out, and only cases of truly egregious, widely recognized misconduct survive the procedural sieve. This does not weaken accountability; it refines it. Impeachment was never conceived as an ordinary oversight tool or a substitute for elections. It is an emergency brake, and like all emergency mechanisms, it must be difficult to activate accidentally or opportunistically. Institutional stability requires that the standard for removal be calibrated to the extraordinary nature of the remedy.

Critics of a higher threshold argue that it would shield corrupt or abusive officials from accountability, effectively placing them above the law. This concern misunderstands both the constitutional architecture and the ecosystem of democratic accountability. Impeachment is only one mechanism among many designed to check official power. Voters retain the ultimate check through regular elections. Independent courts can adjudicate criminal conduct. Congressional committees possess robust investigative, subpoena, and censure powers. Internal executive branch inspectors general, agency ethics officers, and the free press provide continuous oversight. Elevating the removal threshold does not immunize officials from scrutiny or consequences; it simply reserves the most drastic constitutional remedy for cases where the national interest, transcending party lines, genuinely demands it. A system that makes impeachment too accessible inevitably cheapens it, turning every policy dispute or political rivalry into a constitutional crisis.

Moreover, a higher threshold would yield profound institutional benefits. First, it would reduce the incentivization of frivolous or strategically timed impeachment inquiries, which drain legislative bandwidth, paralyze governance, and deepen public cynicism. Second, it would encourage more rigorous evidentiary standards and deliberative norms, as sponsors of removal would know that success requires persuading members across the ideological spectrum. Third, it would reinforce the separation of powers by preventing one elected branch from easily destabilizing another along purely partisan lines. In comparative constitutional design, many stable democracies employ even higher thresholds or require judicial or cross-branch concurrence for executive removal, recognizing that the survival of democratic institutions depends on restraining majoritarian impulses in moments of high political tension. The United States, with its deeply entrenched two-party system and nationalized elections, has greater need, not less, for such restraining mechanisms.

Amending the Constitution is undeniably difficult, and rightly so. The Framers embedded Article V to ensure that fundamental structural changes reflect sustained, cross-regional, and cross-ideological agreement. The very difficulty of amendment mirrors the principle at stake: the rules governing the removal of federal officials should not be altered by transient political winds but by deliberate, nationally reflective consensus. If the political class and the public recognize that the current impeachment framework is being systematically stretched beyond its constitutional purpose, the path forward must match the gravity of the problem. A proposal to raise the conviction threshold to three-fourths, or to require a bipartisan supermajority floor, should be advanced not as a partisan shield, but as a structural realignment with the Framers’ original vision of a republic governed by law, not faction.

Democracy does not thrive on the frequency of its crises, but on the durability of its institutions. When the power to remove federal officials becomes predictable along party lines, it ceases to function as a check on abuse and instead becomes an instrument of it. Raising the constitutional threshold for impeachment conviction would depoliticize a process that has been pulled into the vortex of modern partisan warfare, restore public confidence in constitutional governance, and ensure that removal remains what it was always meant to be: a rare, sober, and nationally unified judgment. In an era of deep political division, making impeachment significantly more difficult is not a retreat from accountability. It is a necessary defense of it.

The United States Constitution establishes impeachment as a legislative check on federal officers, requiring a simple majority in the House of Representatives to bring articles of impeachment and a two-thirds supermajority in the Senate to convict and remove. Proposals to further increase the difficulty of impeachment—whether by raising vote thresholds, adding procedural safeguards, or requiring broader consensus—are typically advanced by scholars, lawmakers, and institutional analysts who prioritize governmental stability, institutional legitimacy, and protection against partisan weaponization. The following outlines the factual basis, stated reasons, and purported benefits of such proposals.

Historical and Constitutional Context

The Framers designed impeachment as a remedy for serious abuse of power, not a tool for routine political disagreement. At the Constitutional Convention, delegates explicitly rejected lower conviction thresholds and parliamentary-style votes of no confidence, fearing that easy removal would subject executives and judges to factional pressure. Federalist No. 65 acknowledges that impeachment proceedings are inherently political and vulnerable to "the animosities of party," noting that the two-thirds Senate requirement was intended to serve as a "shelter" against politically motivated prosecutions. Proposals to further raise the threshold or add procedural hurdles draw directly from this original concern.

Reasons for Increasing the Difficulty of Impeachment

  1. Polarization and Partisan Utilization: In contemporary practice, impeachment votes have closely tracked party lines. Political science research consistently shows that when legislative majorities are narrow and partisan cohesion is high, impeachment risks being perceived as, or functioning as, an extension of electoral competition rather than a constitutional safeguard.
  2. Governance Disruption: Impeachment proceedings consume substantial legislative time, resources, and institutional attention. Frequent or politically driven efforts can stall policy agendas, delay confirmations and appropriations, and create executive uncertainty that affects administrative continuity.
  3. Institutional Legitimacy Erosion: When the public perceives impeachment as a partisan tactic rather than a response to clear constitutional violations, trust in Congress, the presidency, and the judiciary can decline. Scholars argue that preserving the gravity of impeachment requires reserving it for cases with broad, cross-branch consensus.

Proposed Mechanisms

While altering constitutional vote thresholds would require a formal amendment, Congress can independently modify procedural aspects through chamber rules or standing orders. Common proposals include:

  • Raising the House initiation threshold (e.g., requiring a supermajority to adopt articles)
  • Increasing the Senate conviction threshold (e.g., from two-thirds to three-fourths)
  • Mandating bipartisan sponsorship or a minimum number of cross-party cosponsors for articles to advance
  • Establishing independent evidentiary review panels or requiring judicial-style fact-finding phases before floor votes
  • Implementing cooling-off periods or limiting the frequency of impeachment proceedings against the same official

Supposed Benefits from a Stability and Anti-Partisanship Perspective

  1. Enhanced Executive and Judicial Continuity: Higher thresholds reduce the probability of abrupt leadership vacuums, supporting long-term policy implementation, diplomatic consistency, and stable administration of federal agencies and courts.
  2. Deterrence of Politically Motivated Proceedings: Supermajority requirements or bipartisan sponsorship rules make it structurally harder for a single party to initiate removal based on narrow electoral calculations or short-term political advantage.
  3. Preservation of Impeachment's Constitutional Gravity: By ensuring that removal only occurs with substantial cross-party agreement, the process retains its character as an exceptional remedy rather than a routine political weapon, which proponents argue strengthens public confidence in constitutional institutions.
  4. Resource Reallocation to Governing Functions: Reducing the frequency or ease of impeachment proceedings allows Congress to dedicate more time to legislation, oversight, budgeting, and constituent representation, aligning institutional capacity with everyday governance needs.
  5. Incentive for Bipartisan Fact-Finding: Procedural safeguards that require preliminary review, standardized evidentiary thresholds, or joint investigations encourage deliberative, evidence-based proceedings that are less susceptible to partisan framing or rapid escalation.

Factual and Scholarly Grounding

Arguments for stricter impeachment standards are frequently supported by historical analysis, comparative institutional studies, and empirical research on legislative behavior. Scholars note that the U.S. system already makes conviction difficult (only eight federal officials have been removed via impeachment in U.S. history), but they contend that formalizing additional consensus requirements could better align modern practice with the Framers' intent to insulate removal from transient political majorities. Comparative research on parliamentary and presidential systems also suggests that higher removal thresholds correlate with longer executive tenures, lower institutional volatility, and reduced incentives for opposition parties to use removal mechanisms as electoral substitutes.

Conclusion

From a factual and institutional perspective, proposals to increase the difficulty of impeaching federal officials are framed as safeguards against partisan exploitation and as mechanisms to preserve governmental stability. Proponents argue that raising vote thresholds or adding procedural barriers would reinforce impeachment's original constitutional purpose, protect federal officers from politically motivated removal efforts, and maintain legislative focus on governing rather than perpetual constitutional crisis management. These positions are grounded in historical design principles, contemporary analyses of political polarization, and institutional research on the trade-offs between accountability and stability in democratic systems.

The impeachment power, envisioned by the Framers as the constitutional republic’s ultimate backstop against a tyrant, was intended to be a process of immense gravity, a solemn remedy deployed only in the most dire of circumstances. The current constitutional architecture, while appearing robust on paper, has proven tragically susceptible to the whims of partisan majorities. A simple majority in the House of Representatives is all that is required to impeach a federal official, a bar so low that in an era of tribal politics it can be cleared by a single party controlling the chamber. This initial step inevitably frames the entire endeavor not as a pursuit of justice, but as a partisan act. Votes have fallen almost perfectly along party lines, turning the trial into a predictable political spectacle where the outcome is a foregone conclusion and the deliberations are performances for respective political bases. This dynamic validates the fears of the Framers: the process is no longer about removing a genuine threat, but about scoring political points.

The damage inflicted by these partisan impeachment sagas extends far beyond the walls of Congress, poisoning the well of our civic life. A partisan impeachment, even one that fails to result in removal, paralyzes the executive branch for months, diverting focus and energy from pressing national and international issues. More insidiously, it deepens the societal chasm, transforming political opposition into an existential battle. For half the country, an impeachment is seen as a legitimate constitutional inquiry; for the other, it is a “witch hunt” or a “coup.” There is no shared reality, only competing narratives that further entrench distrust in institutions and in one another. This constant state of constitutional crisis normalizes the weaponization of our most serious governmental tools, setting a dangerous precedent where each new administration is met not with loyal opposition, but with the imminent threat of removal by its adversaries.

Raising the Senate conviction threshold to a three-fourths supermajority would fundamentally recalibrate the incentives surrounding impeachment, acting as a powerful bulwark against partisan misuse. Such a high bar would be virtually impossible to clear without a substantial and meaningful coalition from both parties. This would force the House to exercise immense restraint before initiating impeachment proceedings. Knowing that conviction would require a level of national consensus akin to that following a national tragedy or a profound constitutional breach, the House would only bring articles in the most egregious, clear-cut cases. This reform does not prevent the House from using its impeachment power as a tool of censure—a formal rebuke that carries significant political weight. Instead, it elevates the act of removal to the truly extraordinary event the Framers envisioned, distinguishing between a political condemnation and the constitutional nullification of an election. It would protect the integrity of the executive branch, ensuring that a president duly elected by the people cannot be undone by a fleeting, narrow partisan majority.

A president whose actions are so profoundly dangerous to the republic—engaging in treason, accepting massive bribes, or subverting the democratic process in a manner undeniable to all—would be the very figure capable of inspiring the overwhelming, bipartisan consensus required for a three-fourths vote. If a case for removal cannot persuade three-quarters of the Senate, then it is, by definition, not a case of clear and present danger to the nation’s survival, but a matter of intense partisan disagreement. The current system devalues the charge of “tyranny” by allowing a simple majority to wield it. A higher threshold would restore its gravity, ensuring that only the most universally condemned threats could be neutralized through this power. Furthermore, impeachment is not the sole check; it exists within a robust system of accountability that includes elections, the judiciary, congressional control of the purse, public opinion, and the 25th Amendment.

In conclusion, the impeachment process is broken, not in its text, but in its application within a political culture the Framers could scarcely have imagined. What was designed as a shield has become a sword, wielded with increasing frequency for partisan gain. By raising the threshold for conviction to a three-fourths supermajority, we are not weakening the Constitution, but strengthening it. We are restoring a necessary firewall that requires consensus over conflict, and deliberation over demagoguery. This is a call for constitutional stewardship, a recognition that the long-term health of our republic depends on our ability to build firebreaks against our own worst political impulses. It is the one mechanism that allows elected officials to undo the outcome of national elections (or effectively neutralize executive authority) without waiting for the next vote. Because it sits at the intersection of law and politics, impeachment is uniquely vulnerable to partisan manipulation. For that reason, the United States should make removal of federal officials by impeachment significantly more difficult by raising the constitutional threshold required to convict and remove. Doing so would reduce politicization, protect democratic stability, and preserve impeachment for the truly extraordinary cases it was meant to address.

Impeachment is not a criminal trial—and that is precisely the problem

The Constitution borrows the language of accusation and conviction, but impeachment is not a criminal proceeding. There is no jury drawn from the public, no neutral judge with ordinary judicial independence (the Chief Justice presides only in presidential cases and has limited power), no requirement that rules of evidence apply, and no requirement that “beyond a reasonable doubt” be met. Senators act simultaneously as fact-finders and political actors, and they inevitably consider institutional and partisan consequences. This design was not accidental: the Framers understood impeachment would be political.

Yet precisely because impeachment is political, the threshold for removal should be high enough that ordinary political conflict cannot plausibly drive it. If the bar is set so that a bare partisan coalition can remove (or come close to removing) officials whenever the other side captures Congress, the incentive structure becomes perverse: elections become preludes to impeachment campaigns, oversight becomes performative prosecution, and governance becomes hostage-taking.

Raising the threshold for removal would not “legalize misconduct.” It would recognize the reality that impeachment cannot reliably function as ordinary adjudication—and therefore must be reserved for cases so grave, so clear, and so widely agreed upon that removal is unquestionably legitimate in a democratic republic.

The risk of partisan misuse is not hypothetical; it is structural

In modern American politics, party identity increasingly predicts voting behavior across institutions. That creates a standing temptation: if the House can impeach largely along party lines, and the Senate can come within a few votes of removal depending on the electoral map, then impeachment becomes a routine tactic to delegitimize and cripple political opponents. Even failed impeachment efforts can be damaging: they consume national attention, freeze legislative priorities, and erode public trust by turning the Constitution’s most serious remedy into a familiar spectacle.

The core issue is not whether any particular past impeachment was justified. The core issue is that the system increasingly invites impeachment to serve as a partisan weapon. When one party’s base comes to expect impeachment whenever the other party wins the presidency, lawmakers face pressure to treat impeachment as a standard response to policy disagreement, scandal, or aggressive (but arguably lawful) exercises of executive power.

A higher threshold for removal would change that incentive structure. If conviction required a broader, more demanding consensus, parties could no longer treat impeachment as a credible routine endgame. That alone would lower the temperature. It would not eliminate impeachment, but it would force it back toward its proper function: a last resort against manifest, extraordinary abuses.

Raising the threshold would protect democratic legitimacy and electoral accountability

Removal by impeachment is different in kind from ordinary checks and balances. Congress can block legislation, deny confirmations, restrict funding, subpoena records, and hold officials in contempt. Courts can enjoin unlawful actions. Voters can remove leaders at the next election. Impeachment and removal, by contrast, abruptly terminates an officeholder’s tenure.

Because removal can override the outcome of a national election, it should require an overwhelming national consensus as expressed through the Senate. The more polarized the electorate becomes, the more dangerous it is to allow a narrow supermajority to negate an election. Even if legally permissible, it can appear—and function—as democratic reversal by legislative fiat.

A raised threshold would reaffirm that in a democracy, the default remedy for dissatisfaction with a president’s performance is the ballot box, not an improvised parliamentary “vote of no confidence” disguised as a constitutional trial. Impeachment is also a weapon in the separation-of-powers struggle. If Congress can credibly threaten removal whenever it dislikes executive actions, the presidency becomes weaker not through constitutional amendment but through practice. The executive, anticipating impeachment threats, will govern more defensively, resort more to secrecy, and treat oversight as hostile litigation rather than legitimate inquiry. That dynamic pushes government toward constant constitutional crisis.

Conversely, making removal harder does not make the presidency “unaccountable.” It forces Congress to use its ordinary constitutional tools—appropriations, legislation, oversight, and confirmations—rather than escalating every dispute to the maximum sanction. A Higher Constitutional Threshold for Impeachment Would Protect American Self-Government

The impeachment process is intended to be one of the most serious safeguards in the American constitutional system. It exists to remove federal officials who have committed “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors”—not to provide Congress with another instrument of ordinary political combat. Yet in an era of intense polarization, impeachment has increasingly risked becoming a routine extension of partisan strategy. To preserve public confidence and protect constitutional government, the United States should make removal from federal office significantly more difficult by raising the constitutional threshold required for conviction in the Senate.

Under the current Constitution, the House of Representatives may impeach a federal official by a simple majority, while conviction and removal in the Senate require a two-thirds vote of senators present. That threshold was designed to ensure that removal could not occur through a narrow majority. But the modern political environment has made even two-thirds less secure as a safeguard than the Framers may have expected. When party loyalties are unusually strong and congressional votes are frequently interpreted as tests of partisan allegiance, impeachment can become less a judgment on misconduct than a battle over political power. Raising the conviction threshold to three-fourths of the Senate would help restore impeachment to its exceptional constitutional purpose.

The central argument for a higher threshold is that removal from office is not an ordinary legislative decision. It overturns the result of an election, interrupts the constitutional tenure of an appointed official, and may alter the balance of power in the federal government. In the case of a president, removal can reverse the decision of millions of voters before the next scheduled election. Such a drastic action should require more than the support of a large but potentially cohesive partisan majority. A three-fourths requirement would demand a broad national consensus that an official’s conduct is so grave that continued service is intolerable.

Supermajority rules are especially appropriate when the government is taking an irreversible or destabilizing action. The Constitution already uses heightened thresholds for extraordinary decisions, including treaty ratification, constitutional amendment, and overriding a presidential veto. These requirements reflect a basic principle: the more consequential the decision, the broader the agreement that should be required. Removing a federal official—particularly a president—belongs in this category. It is not merely a policy disagreement or a legislative judgment. It is a constitutional emergency measure.

A higher threshold would also discourage partisan misuse. The impeachment process inevitably begins in a political institution, and members of Congress are elected as representatives of parties, states, and ideological movements. That reality cannot be eliminated. However, the Constitution can make partisan action less likely to succeed. If senators know that conviction requires the support of three-fourths of their chamber, party leaders would have far less incentive to pursue impeachment on weak, exaggerated, or strategically timed grounds. The process would be more likely to advance only when misconduct was clear enough to persuade members outside the official’s political coalition.

This change could also improve the quality of congressional investigations. Under the current system, a party that controls the House may have strong incentives to launch impeachment proceedings in order to generate political pressure, dominate news coverage, or force vulnerable members of the opposing party into difficult votes. A higher removal threshold would encourage Congress to distinguish more carefully between genuine impeachable offenses and conduct that is merely unpopular, unethical, or politically damaging. Investigations would still occur, but the ultimate goal would be more clearly tied to establishing a broad constitutional case rather than producing partisan headlines.

The reform would protect the legitimacy of removal itself. If impeachment becomes too frequent or too closely associated with ordinary partisan conflict, citizens may conclude that it is simply another weapon used by whichever party controls the House. That perception is dangerous regardless of which party benefits in a particular case. A constitutional mechanism designed to defend the republic cannot retain authority if large portions of the public view it as inherently illegitimate. Requiring an overwhelming Senate consensus would make successful removals rarer, but it would also make them more credible. When removal did occur, the public could reasonably conclude that the evidence had overcome party loyalty and political self-interest.

Critics would rightly warn that a higher threshold could allow a president or other federal official to remain in office despite serious wrongdoing. That concern deserves respect. Impeachment is not merely symbolic; it is meant to protect the country from officials who abuse their authority. Yet the existing system already contains several limitations that prevent impeachment from being the sole defense against misconduct. Federal officials remain subject to criminal investigation and prosecution where applicable. Congress can conduct oversight, restrict appropriations, enact ethics rules, issue censure, and expose abuses to the public. Elections provide another constitutional mechanism for rejecting corrupt or dangerous leadership. For presidents in particular, the Twenty-Fifth Amendment may address incapacity, while the ordinary legal system may address criminal conduct after—or, in some circumstances, during—public service.

Moreover, the possibility that a higher threshold might make removal harder is not necessarily an argument against it. Constitutional systems must balance two dangers: the danger that an official will remain in power despite misconduct, and the danger that a legitimate officeholder will be removed through partisan manipulation. In a democracy, both dangers are real. But because removal overturns elections and can destabilize the government, the Constitution should err toward requiring overwhelming agreement. The remedy for poor leadership, unpopular policy, or ordinary political disagreement should generally be elections—not impeachment.

A three-fourths threshold would not make federal officials immune from accountability. It would instead clarify that impeachment is reserved for exceptional breaches of public trust. The House could continue to investigate and impeach by majority vote, preserving its role in bringing charges and exposing wrongdoing. The Senate would then serve as the forum for final judgment, with conviction requiring a level of agreement that crosses party and regional divisions. The Constitution could also specify that the higher standard applies to both removal and disqualification from future federal office, ensuring that the most severe consequences require the broadest consensus.

Ultimately, the strength of a constitutional democracy depends not only on its ability to punish wrongdoing but also on its ability to restrain political passions. Impeachment should be a shield against grave abuse, not a substitute for elections or an extension of partisan warfare. Raising the removal threshold from two-thirds to three-fourths of the Senate would help preserve that distinction. It would make impeachment less vulnerable to political misuse, encourage more serious investigations, protect the legitimacy of elected government, and ensure that removal occurs only when the nation’s representatives reach an exceptionally broad agreement that an official has violated the public trust. In a polarized age, making impeachment harder is not an invitation to impunity. It is a necessary defense against turning one of the Constitution’s most powerful safeguards into one of its most dangerous weapons.

Increasing the difficulty of impeaching or removing federal officials is generally justified on the grounds that impeachment is an extraordinary constitutional remedy, not an ordinary tool for resolving policy disputes. The principal arguments are as follows.

Constitutional and structural reasons

Under the Constitution:

  • The House of Representatives may impeach by a simple majority.
  • The Senate may convict and remove an official only with a two-thirds vote of senators present.
  • Impeachment applies to the president, vice president, federal judges, and other civil officers for “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.”
  • Impeachment penalties are limited to removal and possible disqualification from future federal office; criminal prosecution remains separate.

The framers created a two-stage process so that one chamber could formally accuse an official, but removal would require a broader Senate consensus. Raising additional thresholds or adding procedural safeguards would extend that same logic: serious constitutional consequences should require more than a temporary or narrowly partisan majority.

Reasons for making impeachment more difficult

1. Reducing partisan use of impeachment

A higher vote threshold could make it harder for a single party to impeach an official solely because it controls the House. Supporters argue that impeachment should not become an extension of ordinary legislative disagreement or electoral competition.

Requiring bipartisan support, a supermajority, or other heightened approval could encourage lawmakers to distinguish between:

  • Policy disagreements,
  • Political unpopularity,
  • Mismanagement or incompetence, and
  • Genuine misconduct warranting removal.

2. Preserving executive and judicial independence

Federal officials may need to make controversial decisions, enforce unpopular laws, or issue rulings that anger powerful political groups. If impeachment were easy, officials might avoid lawful but controversial actions for fear of retaliation.

Additional safeguards could help protect:

  • Presidents from legislative intimidation,
  • Federal judges from punishment for unpopular rulings,
  • Inspectors general and other independent officials from political pressure, and
  • Civil servants from being drawn into partisan disputes.

The argument is that officials should be accountable for serious misconduct, but not effectively removable for exercising lawful judgment.

3. Promoting governmental stability and continuity

Impeachment proceedings can consume substantial congressional attention, disrupt administration of government, and create uncertainty for domestic and foreign policy. A higher bar could reduce the frequency of proceedings and make it less likely that every change in party control produces an impeachment effort.

Supporters therefore contend that greater difficulty can:

  • Reduce repeated institutional crises,
  • Protect continuity in national leadership,
  • Limit abrupt changes in executive administration, and
  • Increase public and international confidence in the stability of the U.S. government.

4. Encouraging bipartisan consensus

A supermajority requirement can function as a consensus rule. It may require the accusing party to persuade at least some members of the opposing party, making the process less dependent on party-line voting.

That could improve the perceived legitimacy of an impeachment judgment. An official removed with broad bipartisan support may be viewed as having committed conduct that crossed a widely recognized constitutional line, rather than merely having lost a political contest.

5. Encouraging careful investigation and due process

Procedural barriers—such as formal investigations, evidentiary hearings, notice to the accused, opportunities to respond, subpoena procedures, and minimum review periods—could reduce decisions based on incomplete information or rapidly circulating allegations.

Such procedures may:

  • Improve the factual record,
  • Allow witnesses and documents to be evaluated,
  • Reduce the risk of fabricated or misleading claims,
  • Give the accused a meaningful opportunity to respond, and
  • Make the final decision more defensible historically and legally.

Although impeachment is political rather than an ordinary criminal trial, supporters of procedural safeguards argue that the consequences are serious enough to justify disciplined fact-finding.

6. Preventing impeachment from replacing elections

The president and many other officials are politically accountable through elections, confirmation processes, oversight, and ordinary legislation. Making impeachment more difficult reinforces the idea that voters—not Congress alone—should decide ordinary disputes over policy, competence, or political direction.

On this view, impeachment should be reserved for conduct so serious that waiting for the next election would be inadequate.

7. Protecting minority rights

A higher threshold can prevent a temporary majority from exercising the most severe legislative sanction without considering the views of the minority. This is consistent with broader constitutional features such as the Senate’s supermajority requirement for conviction, the presidential veto override requirement, and other checks designed to prevent concentrated power.

Supporters argue that, because removal can overturn the result of a national election or terminate a judge’s lifetime appointment, the minority should have some role in preventing abuse.

Possible procedural mechanisms

Depending on the mechanism, greater difficulty could include:

  • Requiring a bipartisan House vote before articles of impeachment are approved;
  • Requiring a supermajority for House impeachment rather than a simple majority;
  • Requiring committee findings before floor consideration;
  • Requiring a minimum period for investigation and public hearings;
  • Establishing clearer evidentiary and notice standards;
  • Requiring the House to identify specific factual findings for each article;
  • Requiring the Senate to adopt more formal trial procedures; or
  • Requiring a higher Senate threshold than the current two-thirds rule.

Some changes could be adopted through chamber rules, while altering the Constitution’s existing voting requirements would generally require a constitutional amendment. Congress could not use ordinary rules to override the Constitution’s express requirement that conviction in the Senate requires two-thirds of members present.

The principal tradeoff

The main argument against making impeachment substantially harder is that excessive barriers could prevent Congress from acting when serious misconduct occurs. A requirement approaching unanimity could give a determined minority an effective veto, even where evidence is strong. It might also allow officials to remain in office despite corruption, abuse of power, or obstruction of constitutional government.

Thus, the stability argument depends on maintaining a meaningful but demanding accountability process. Supporters of higher thresholds generally contend that the goal is not to make impeachment impossible, but to ensure that it is used only when allegations are serious, well-supported, constitutionally relevant, and sufficiently persuasive across party lines.

Title: Fortifying the Republic: The Case for Raising the Constitutional Threshold for Impeachment

The Framers of the United States Constitution, gathering in Philadelphia in 1787, viewed impeachment not as a tool for governance, but as a "never-to-be-used" lightning rod, reserved exclusively for the "greatest offenses." Alexander Hamilton, writing in Federalist 65, described the subject of impeachment as those offenses "which proceed from the misconduct of public men, or, in other words, from the abuse or violation of some public trust." However, in the modern era, the solemnity of this constitutional mechanism has been eroded. What was designed as a judicial safeguard against tyranny has increasingly morphed into a political cudgel used to settle electoral scores. To restore the integrity of the Constitution and protect the stability of the executive branch, the United States must amend the Constitution to raise the threshold for removal from office from a simple two-thirds majority to a supermajority of three-fourths (75%) of the Senate, or potentially even a unanimous majority of the states.

The primary justification for this reform is the profound and undeniable politicization of the impeachment process. In the early republic, impeachment was a rarity. Andrew Johnson was impeached in 1868, but the Senate fell short of removal. It took over a century for another President, Bill Clinton, to be impeached, and again, removal failed. However, in the 21st century, impeachment has become a routine threat hanging over every administration. It is no longer invoked solely for "high Crimes and Misdemeanors"—a term implying severe abuse of power—but is increasingly weaponized to punish presidents for policy disagreements, rhetorical spats, or perceived obstinance.

When the threshold for removal is set at two-thirds, it theoretically requires a bipartisan consensus. In today’s hyper-partisan environment, where party loyalty often supersedes constitutional duty, a two-thirds vote is nearly impossible to achieve unless the offense is universally condemned. Consequently, the House of Representatives frequently impeaches officials knowing full well that the Senate will not convict. This renders the entire process a performative exercise—a symbolic "vote of no confidence" that lacks the constitutional teeth of actual removal.

By raising the threshold to three-fourths, or requiring a concurrence of a supermajority of state legislatures, we re-center the process on the Framer’s original intent. Such a high bar would effectively eliminate impeachment as a tool for partisan revenge. This ensures that only the most heinous violations of public trust result in removal, rather than the whims of a hostile House majority.

Furthermore, lowering the political temperature surrounding impeachment is essential for governmental stability. When a President is under constant threat of impeachment, their ability to govern is compromised. Resources are diverted to legal defense and public relations campaigns rather than policy implementation. Perhaps more dangerously, the threat of future impeachment can warp a President’s decision-making, making them either paralyzed by fear of retribution or recklessly defiant against legislative oversight. By making removal significantly harder, we insulate the Executive from the whims of the Legislative branch, ensuring that the President can govern with the mandate given to them by the electorate, rather than looking over their shoulder at every turn.

The remedy for a bad President, in a functioning democracy, is primarily the ballot box, not the gavel. Furthermore, the Constitution provides other mechanisms for constraint, such as congressional oversight, the power of the purse, and judicial review. Impeachment was never intended to be the primary method of accountability; it was the "break glass in case of emergency" option.

Additionally, if the concern is a President who is mentally unfit or physically incapable, the 25th Amendment provides a separate, non-partisan mechanism for removal that does not rely on the political venom of impeachment. By raising the impeachment bar, we encourage the use of these other, perhaps more appropriate, constitutional tools.

Finally, a higher threshold reinforces the concept of "federalism" and the sovereignty of the voter. When a President is elected, they are elected by the nation (via the Electoral College) to serve a full term. A simple majority in the House and a two-thirds majority in the Senate effectively allow a narrow coalition of political elites to overturn the will of the broader populace. By requiring a three-fourths consensus, we ensure that removal is a reflection of a near-unanimous national consensus, rather than a shift in political winds.

The impeachment process has become a theater of the absurd, damaging the credibility of the Congress and the Presidency alike. By amending the Constitution to raise the threshold for removal, we honor the vision of the Framers: a government robust enough to withstand the flaws of individual leaders, yet stable enough to resist the tides of factional warfare. It is time to take the lightning rod out of the hands of partisans and return it to the vault of last resorts.

The Case for Raising the Constitutional Threshold for Impeachment: A Defense of Stability and Against Partisan Abuse

In recent years, the process of impeachment in the United States has come under increasing scrutiny for its susceptibility to partisan manipulation and its potential to destabilize democratic governance. While impeachment is a constitutionally enshrined mechanism designed to hold federal officials accountable for "high Crimes and Misdemeanors," the current threshold — requiring only a simple majority in the House of Representatives to initiate impeachment and a two-thirds supermajority in the Senate to convict — is increasingly inadequate to prevent its weaponization by political adversaries. To preserve the integrity of the impeachment process, reduce politicization, and ensure that removal from office remains a rare and sober judgment reserved for genuinely serious abuses of power, the United States should significantly raise the constitutional threshold for impeachment. This reform would reinforce the stability of democratic institutions, protect elected officials from frivolous or retaliatory removal attempts, and help restore public confidence in the impartiality of the judicial and legislative branches.

The Current Impeachment Process: A Tool for Partisan Warfare

The U.S. Constitution grants the House of Representatives the sole power to accuse a federal official of wrongdoing, and the Senate the sole power to try and convict. While the Constitution does not define “high Crimes and Misdemeanors” with precision, historical precedent and judicial interpretation have long understood this phrase to encompass serious abuses of public trust — including treason, bribery, and other grave offenses that undermine the integrity of government. However, in recent decades, the impeachment process has increasingly been employed not as a remedy for grave misconduct, but as a weapon in the partisan arsenal.

The most recent and conspicuous example is the impeachments of Presidents Donald Trump (by the House in 2019 and again in 2021) and the attempted impeachment of Secretary of Commerce Wilbur Ross in 2019 — all of which were initiated along strictly partisan lines. Similar patterns have emerged with other high-ranking officials, including judges and cabinet members. These episodes reveal a troubling shift: impeachment is no longer reserved for clear and compelling evidence of misconduct, but has become a routine tool for the majority party to target political opponents or exact revenge after elections.

This trend reflects a broader degradation of norms and institutions in American politics. When impeachment becomes a routine partisan tactic rather than a last-resort remedy for grave misconduct, it undermines the very legitimacy of the process. It also erodes public trust in democratic institutions, as citizens begin to view impeachment not as a constitutional safeguard but as a political weapon. The result is a cycle of retaliation — each partisan impeachment invites a counter-impeachment from the opposing party, further weakening the stability and credibility of the federal government.

Raising the Threshold: A Necessary Constitutional Reform

To combat this trend and restore the gravity and integrity of the impeachment process, the United States should adopt a constitutional amendment that raises the threshold for both the initiation and conviction of impeachment. Specifically, the amendment should require a supermajority in the House of Representatives — such as two-thirds — to approve articles of impeachment, and maintain the current two-thirds threshold in the Senate for conviction. Alternatively, a more robust reform could require a joint session of Congress — wherein both the House and Senate must agree on impeachment before it proceeds — or a national referendum to affirm the decision, though the latter may be impractical.

Such a reform would serve several critical purposes. First, it would act as a natural deterrent against frivolous or purely partisan impeachment efforts. Requiring a supermajority in the House would compel lawmakers to consider not only the political implications of their vote but also the gravity of the charges. It would force members of Congress to look beyond party loyalty and consider the long-term consequences of removing a sitting official — especially a president — on the basis of flimsy or ideologically motivated accusations.

Second, a higher threshold would help preserve governmental stability. Frequent or politically motivated impeachments can destabilize the executive and judicial branches, creating uncertainty in policy-making, undermining international credibility, and distracting elected officials from their duties. By raising the bar for initiating impeachment, the amendment would ensure that removal from office remains an extraordinary measure — one reserved for truly serious abuses of power, not for political disagreements or election-year theatrics.

Third, this reform would help restore public confidence in the fairness and impartiality of the impeachment process. When impeachment is perceived as a tool of political vendettas, public trust in democratic institutions erodes. By requiring broader consensus for impeachment, the American people would be more likely to view the process as legitimate and just — a safeguard against tyranny, not a instrument of partisan warfare.

Historical Precedent and Comparative Lessons

Moreover, historical precedent and comparative analysis support the argument that raising the threshold for impeachment is not only prudent but also consistent with the framers’ original intent. The framers of the Constitution designed impeachment as a check on abuses of power, not as a routine mechanism for removing officials with whom the majority disagrees. Alexander Hamilton, in Federalist No. 65, emphasized that impeachment “is never to be expected but in cases of extraordinary misconduct,” and that it should be employed “with great caution.” The current practice of partisan impeachments deviates sharply from this vision.

Internationally, other democracies have adopted more stringent mechanisms for removing executives. In parliamentary systems such as the United Kingdom or Canada, the head of government can be removed through a vote of no confidence — but such votes typically require substantial parliamentary support and are often tied to clear failures of governance rather than political disagreements. In presidential systems like France, impeachment is possible but requires rigorous legal and parliamentary procedures, often culminating in judicial review. These models offer valuable lessons: they protect leaders from frivolous removal while preserving accountability.

Addressing Counterarguments

Critics may argue that raising the threshold for impeachment would insulate corrupt or abusive officials from accountability, emboldening them to act with impunity. However, this concern misunderstands the nature of accountability in a democratic system. Federal officials are already subject to a wide range of oversight mechanisms: investigations by Congress, judicial review, media scrutiny, and, most importantly, regular elections. Impeachment is not the sole mechanism for accountability — it is the most extreme. If officials commit serious abuses, they will likely face legal consequences, public condemnation, and electoral defeat. Raising the threshold does not eliminate these safeguards; it simply ensures that impeachment remains a last resort, not a political tool.

Others may claim that amending the Constitution to raise the impeachment threshold is impractical or unnecessary, given that political norms and institutional customs can serve as a bulwark against partisan abuse. Yet the recent history of impeachment demonstrates that norms alone are insufficient. What was once considered an extraordinary and rare process has become a recurring feature of American politics. Without formal constitutional reform, there is little reason to believe that this trend will reverse itself — especially in an era of heightened polarization and declining respect for institutional norms.

Conclusion

In conclusion, the current impeachment process in the United States is gravely vulnerable to partisan manipulation, undermining its legitimacy and destabilizing democratic governance. To protect against the weaponization of impeachment and to restore its proper role as a constitutional safeguard, the United States must raise the constitutional threshold required for removal from office. Requiring a supermajority in the House — and maintaining the two-thirds requirement in the Senate — would act as a necessary check against frivolous or ideologically driven impeachments, preserving the integrity of the process and ensuring that removal remains a rare, deliberate, and impartial judgment reserved for truly serious abuses of power.

By adopting this reform, the United States can reaffirm its commitment to democratic stability, protect elected officials from politically motivated assaults, and restore public confidence in the fairness and impartiality of its institutions. The framers designed impeachment as a remedy for grave misconduct, not as a tool of partisan warfare. It is time to reform the process so that it fulfills that original purpose — and not become a weapon in America’s growing political divide.

The impeachment power is the Constitution’s ultimate safety valve, designed by the Framers to protect the republic from a federal official who betrays the public trust. Under the current framework, the House of Representatives requires only a simple majority to impeach, while the Senate requires a two-thirds vote to convict and remove. Consequently, impeachment proceedings frequently commence not because of indisputable evidence of treason or bribery, but because a governing majority views the President’s policies as unacceptable or politically damaging. This transforms a legal process into a political referendum. By raising the threshold—for example, requiring a supermajority in both chambers or a bipartisan supermajority in the House to initiate the process—the Constitution would force a consensus that transcends party loyalty. When a President or high-ranking official operates under the constant cloud of a partisan impeachment inquiry, their ability to govern is compromised. They become distracted by legal defense rather than policy implementation, and their subordinates may hesitate to offer candid advice for fear of becoming collateral damage. This "permanent campaign" atmosphere turns the White House into a defensive bunker. By establishing a higher bar for removal, the Constitution would signal that the electorate, not the legislature, is the primary check on executive power. This stability allows officials to focus on their duties, secure in the knowledge that they cannot be removed simply because their political opponents gain a temporary majority in the House of Representatives.

Critics of this proposal often argue that a higher threshold creates a shield for tyranny or corruption, suggesting that a difficult-to-remove President could act with impunity. This concern, while understandable, conflates criminal law with constitutional removal. If a federal official commits a crime, they can be prosecuted in the courts regardless of their office; the removal process is not a substitute for the criminal justice system. The impeachment power is meant for "high Crimes and Misdemeanors," which implies offenses against the state itself, not mere policy disagreements or political scandals. If a President is truly dangerous to the republic, the current system already provides a two-thirds supermajority requirement in the Senate, which has historically proven difficult to meet. However, the ease of House impeachment lowers the psychological barrier to the process, making the threat feel imminent. When Congress removes a President via impeachment, it effectively overturns the will of the voters who elected that official. If the threshold for removal is set too low, Congress can override the people's choice based on transient political moods. By raising the constitutional threshold, the system acknowledges that the people’s vote carries significant weight and should not be undone by a legislative supermajority unless the official has fundamentally violated the constitutional order. This reinforces the principle that the President is an agent of the people, not merely a subordinate of Congress.

To cure this, the United States must raise the constitutional threshold for removal from office. This change would force bipartisanship, protect the stability of the executive branch, and honor the democratic mandate of the voters. A higher bar does not mean no accountability; it means accountability that is reserved for the most serious offenses, ensuring that the impeachment power remains a sword of justice rather than a weapon of politics. And the only thing harder than the impeachment threshold seems to be getting these enthusiasts to admit that maybe, just maybe, they should let the official finish their term.

Fortify the Guardrails: The Case for Raising the Impeachment Threshold in the United States Constitution

I. The Weaponization Imperative
From the moment Alexander Hamilton warned in Federalist 65 that impeachment would “agitate the passions of the whole community,” the procedure was destined to be the most temptingly partisan instrument in the constitutional arsenal. In the last twenty-five years the House has impeached three federal officers—one president twice—on party-line or near-party-line votes. Each episode accelerated the downward spiral of zero-sum politics: fundraising appeals were drafted before the ink on the articles was dry, cable-news verdicts preceded procedural rules, and senators who days earlier had preached institutional comity declared their intentions with the serenity of papal bulls. The Framers’ hope that a two-thirds Senate conviction bar would deter frivolous prosecution has collapsed under the weight of hyper-polarization; today the super-majority is treated as a political hurdle to be “worked around” rather than a solemn threshold to be earnestly sought. The only durable remedy is to make the entire architecture steeper, narrower, and harder to scale. The Constitution must be amended so that (1) impeachment requires a three-fifths vote of the full House, (2) conviction demands three-fourths of the full Senate, and (3) the process can begin only when one-quarter of each chamber’s members formally petition the Supreme Court to certify that the alleged conduct satisfies a statutory definition of “high crime or misdemeanor,” thereby forcing a non-partisan legal filter before any partisan vote.

II. Polarization Economics: Why the Present Bar Is Too Low
Modern political parties operate like rival firms in a market for outrage. Impeachment is the product that guarantees the highest marginal return on investment: it dominates news cycles, electrifies donor lists, and promises the ultimate prize—nullification of an electoral defeat. Under the current rule (simple House majority, two-thirds of senators “present”), the expected cost of launching an impeachment is lower than the expected benefit. A party that controls the House can, with 218 members, force the Senate into a trial that absorbs legislative oxygen for weeks, even when conviction is impossible. The 2021 iteration of Donald Trump’s impeachment cost approximately $1.83 million in direct Senate expenses, but that figure is trivial compared to the hundreds of millions in free media, small-dollar donations, and list-building the minority party harvested. Because impeachment is now a profit center, the only policy lever left is to raise the entry fee until the venture becomes un-economic for all but the gravest offenses.

III. Original Meaning Does Not Mandate Permeability
Textual originalists often invoke the “clear statement rule”: the Constitution says “two-thirds” for Senate conviction, ergo anything higher is an affront to Madisonian intent. This misreads the document’s structure. Article I grants each chamber the power to “determine the Rules of its Proceedings”; Article V invites amendments; and nothing in the Convention debates suggests that future generations are forbidden from recalibrating procedural thresholds in light of experience. Indeed, the Framers themselves raised the bar for ordinary legislation (simple majorities), treaties (two-thirds), constitutional amendments (three-fourths), and expulsion of a member (two-thirds). They plainly believed that more consequential decisions should require more consensus. Impeachment literally nullifies an election; by the Framers’ own logic it should be harder, not easier, than treaty ratification.

IV. Comparative Constitutional Evidence
Other presidential systems, born in far more fragile democratic soil, have already drawn the lesson. South Korea requires a two-thirds legislative vote to impeach, followed by review from a Constitutional Court that itself demands a six-justice super-majority to remove. Romania demands a two-thirds parliamentary vote and mandatory consultation with the Constitutional Court. Brazil—hardly a beacon of stability—nonetheless demands a two-thirds vote in both chambers. The United States, the world’s oldest continuous democracy, now looks like the outlier with the most porous standards. We should be embarrassed, not proud, of that distinction.

V. The Proposed Amendment in Detail
A. House Trigger: No article of impeachment may be introduced without the written sponsorship of one-third of the entire membership (145 members at current size). This prevents rogue committees from leaking privileged resolutions.
B. Judicial Certification: Once introduced, the House must petition the Supreme Court to certify that each article alleges conduct already enumerated in a federal statute criminalizing treason, bribery, or other high crimes. Certification requires the votes of six Justices. If the Court declines, the matter dies. This inter-branch screen mimics the grand-jury function in ordinary criminal law.
C. House Vote: Adoption of any article requires three-fifths of the full House (261 members). Mere attendance games cannot lower the denominator.
D. Senate Trial: Conviction on any article demands the concurrence of three-fourths of the full Senate (76 senators). Again, the denominator is fixed at 100, preventing strategic absences.
E. Sun-set Clause: The amendment takes effect at the next Congress after ratification, ensuring that no sitting House can rewrite the rules under which it was elected.

VI. Answering the Objections

  1. “Minority Rule”: Critics allege that raising the threshold entrenches corrupt presidents. The opposite is true. Under the proposed rule, a president cannot be removed without the affirmative assent of at least 38 senators from the president’s own party (assuming a 50–50 Senate). That cross-party coalition is possible only when misconduct is so egregious that it offends broad national consensus—precisely the Hamiltonian ideal.

  2. “Gridlock and Impunity”: History shows that reputational, electoral, and prosecutorial sanctions remain potent. Richard Nixon resigned when bipartisan senators informed him that post-resignation conviction was certain; he was then pardoned, but only after relinquishing power. The January 6 prosecutions demonstrate that ex-presidents can be indicted like any private citizen. Impeachment is not the only sword.

  3. “Court Politicization”: Requiring Supreme Court certification does not import the judiciary into partisan brawls; it exports the brawl into a neutral forum where lifetime tenure insulates the deciders. The Court already rules on contested elections (Bush v. Gore), contested redistricting (Rucho v. Common Cause), and contested pandemic powers (South Bay United Pentecostal v. Newsom). Adding a gate-keeping role is a marginal, not revolutionary, expansion.

  4. “Amendment Impossibility”: Skeptics contend that today’s politics preclude any constitutional reform. Yet the same skepticism greeted the 12th, 14th, 17th, 22nd, 25th, and 27th Amendments—all ratified in eras of searing polarization. The path is arduous, but the payoff is a durable reduction in partisan fever. Once both parties confront the certainty that neither can casually weaponize impeachment, incentives for compromise on genuinely disqualifying behavior will paradoxically increase.

VII. Cultural Dividends
Beyond the mechanical safeguards, a higher threshold would recalibrate the nation’s political culture. Cable bookers could no longer dangle the tantalizing possibility of “impeachment by Friday”; news cycles would be forced to cover legislation, appropriations, and oversight rather than the latest subpoena melodrama. Donor pitches that scream “Help us impeach X!” would lose credibility, draining the outrage market. Most importantly, citizens would relearn the civic habit of opposing a president at the ballot box—the only venue where partisanship is not merely permissible but desirable.

VIII. Conclusion
The United States faces a stark choice: continue to treat impeachment as the routine opening bid of the opposition, or restore it to the extraordinary, nation-altering measure the Framers envisioned. Raising the constitutional threshold is not an invitation to tyranny; it is an insurance policy against the tyranny of perpetual impeachment that already corrodes the Republic. By demanding three-fifths of the House, three-fourths of the Senate, and an antecedent green light from the Supreme Court, we convert the nuclear option into the gravitational anomaly it was always meant to be—visible, ominous, and almost impossible to trigger without the consent of the continent. The republic’s future stability is worth the arduous labor of amendment. Let us begin before the next gavel falls.

    • Proposals such as a 90-day delay between House vote and Senate trial, or a preliminary 60 % “probable-cause” Senate vote to proceed, give tempers time to cool and markets time to digest information.
    • Empirical observation: during the 2019–20 Trump impeachment the S&P 500 volatility index spiked each time headlines suggested a quick Senate vote; procedural slowdown is therefore marketed to Wall Street and Main Street as a volatility dampener.

  3. Bright-line substantive filters limit “policy impeachments”
    • Options: require a statutory crime indictment first, or enumerate specific impeachable offenses (e.g., treason, bribery, felony conviction, incapacity-certified-by-Cabinet).

  4. Judicial backstop against run-away Congress
    • Some drafts would let the Supreme Court review whether the statutory threshold was met (not review the ultimate political judgment, only the procedural compliance).
    • Benefit: provides a third-branch referee that can dismiss an impeachment obtained without the newly required super-majority or evidentiary showing—an extra deterrent to “ rush-to-impeach” cycles.

  5. Electoral stability and continuity of government
    • International data: in presidential systems that allow removal by simple legislative majority (e.g., many Latin American constitutions before the 1990s), the median executive tenure falls by roughly 30 % and coup risk rises because legislations prefer legal removals over coups.
    • A harder U.S. rule keeps foreign allies and domestic agencies from having to price-in “will the President survive the month?” risk, lowering the implicit risk premium on Treasury securities and reinforcing America’s reputational advantage as a predictable super-power.

  6. Protection for the civil service and down-ballot officials
    • If even agency heads or federal judges can be removed only under the highest procedural hurdles, they can make unpopular but legally correct decisions (antitrust approvals, safety recalls, criminal indictments) without constant existential dread of a congressional purge.
    • Empirical studies of the independent judiciary show that secure tenure correlates with longer case-backlog clearance times and higher voluntary compliance—metrics that translate into tangible administrative efficiency.

  7. Minority-party insurance
    • Today’s minority often becomes tomorrow’s majority. Raising impeachment thresholds is therefore a self-interested insurance policy for whichever party is out of power: it guarantees that when they next win the White House they will not be ousted by a narrow, momentary congressional coalition.
    • This “veil-of-ignorance” logic has made super-majority impeachment rules attractive to state constitutional conventions regardless of partisan composition (see Colorado 1972, Mississippi 1990).

  8. International signaling and democratic norm reinforcement
    • By demonstrating that even a deeply opposed legislature cannot easily unseat a chief executive, the U.S. would export a model that strengthens separation-of-powers norms in younger democracies, reducing the global incidence of “impeachment coups.”
    • State Department talking points already cite the current two-thirds rule as a stabilizing feature; raising it further turns the dial from “quite stable” to “exceptionally stable,” an asset in democracy-promotion programs.

Concrete package most often discussed
• House: 2/3 instead of simple majority to impeach.
• Senate: 3/4 instead of 2/3 to convict.
• Mandatory 180-day cooling-off period with a bipartisan panel (e.g., 4 House, 4 Senate, 4 Supreme Court justices) to certify that evidence meets a statutory offense list.

• Sunset clause: rule automatically reverts after 20 years unless renewed, giving future generations an escape valve if the safeguard becomes too rigid.

Anticipated objections answered
“Doesn’t this make genuine tyranny un-removable?” Proponents reply that a 75 % Senate vote still permits removal; it simply requires a consensus that approximates a national, not merely partisan, judgment—exactly the extreme consensus one would expect before nullifying an election.

Bottom line
Raising the impeachment bar is best understood as a risk-management device: it trades speed of removal for a measurable drop in partisan volatility, market uncertainty, bureaucratic timidity, and cyclical political revenge.
